desc:
Consider the sums nums[i] + nums[j] over all pairs of positions i < j. Sort these sums in non-decreasing order (equal sums are listed as many times as they occur) and return the k-th one, counting from 1.

nums = [1, 4, 2, 3], k = 4
all pair sums sorted: 3, 4, 5, 5, 6, 7
result = 5

There can be about n²/2 pair sums, so listing them is too slow.
hints: Generating and sorting all pair sums costs O(n² log n) time and O(n²) memory. Try to avoid listing them.
Binary search on the answer value x: if you can count how many pair sums are at most x, the k-th smallest is the smallest x whose count is at least k.
Count pairs with sum ≤ x on the sorted array with two pointers in O(n): as i grows, the largest valid partner index j only moves left.
editorial: Sort nums. Define count(x) as the number of pairs i < j with sum at most x; it is non-decreasing in x. The answer is the smallest x with count(x) ≥ k, and it is always an actual pair sum. So binary search on x between the smallest possible sum a[0] + a[1] and the largest a[n-2] + a[n-1].

To evaluate count(x) keep j at the last index and sweep i from the left: while a[i] + a[j] > x decrease j; if j > i, the element i pairs with every index in i+1..j, so add j - i. Since a[i] grows with i, the boundary j never moves right, and one evaluation takes O(n).

Total time is O(n log n) for the sort plus O(n log R) for the search, where R ≈ 4 × 10<sup>9</sup> is the range of sums (about 32 iterations). Memory is O(1) extra. The same “binary search on the answer + two pointers to count” template solves k-th smallest pair distance and k-th smallest in sorted matrices.
time: O(n log n + n log R)
